description: Hey! We are Nacho, Álvaro, Raúl, Maken and Paula. We are 42 students, space enthusiasts and we love Mars!!!
summary: A signal takes 3 to 22 minutes between Mars and Earth, so astronauts on a spacewalk must decide alone. ARIADNE is the offline field tool they would carry. It is a layered map of Jezero crater built from real NASA data (HiRISE imagery and terrain, THEMIS thermal inertia, CRISM minerals, USGS geology, MEDA weather, DONKI space weather). It plans the lowest-energy walking route for a suited astronaut at 0.38 g using the Pandolf model. The route avoids steep slopes, loose sand and large rocks, and a safe-return limit shrinks as the EVA clock runs. Several phones, tablets and a laptop share one plan over local Wi-Fi with no internet. The shared plan includes zone and equipment locks, crew positions, and a shared field log whose hazard reports reroute everyone else. A Mars clock replays real weather sols, and a dust-storm and solar-storm drill turns the map into a go/no-go decision. Every value is labelled measured, derived, modelled or simulated, so the crew knows how far to trust it. ARIADNE answers three questions: where do we walk, can we get back, and what do we do if a storm arrives?
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ARIADNE is an offline EVA (spacewalk) planning and field-coordination app for Jezero crater, Mars. It covers a 7.1 x 3.9 km zone on a 20 m grid. The default traverse runs from the Three Forks sample depot to Cheyava Falls, where Perseverance found a potential biosignature: 7.28 km, about 2 h 32 min on foot.

HOW IT WORKS

- Route: Dijkstra over a cost grid built from the HiRISE DTM (slope, relief), THEMIS thermal inertia (loose sand vs. rock) and rock hazards. Slopes over 18 degrees are forbidden. Energy uses the Pandolf equation scaled to Mars gravity, with an 80 kg crew member carrying a 50 kg load. A reverse Dijkstra from the habitat gives a safe-return envelope that shrinks as the EVA clock runs.

- Field network: a laptop acts as a hub on local Wi-Fi. Phones, tablets and the laptop share one ordered plan over WebSockets. The plan holds leased locks on zones and equipment, crew positions, measured latency and an append-only field log (faults, hazards, deviations, samples). A hazard reported by one astronaut reroutes the others. If the hub drops, devices keep working and catch up later.

- Environment: a Mars clock (NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm) that replays real MEDA sols, plus 36 layers in 6 categories: navigation, topography, geology, meteorology, atmosphere, radiation. It adds a dust-storm hazard and a solar-storm drill based on the May 2024 event. Every value carries a provenance tag: MEASURED, DERIVED, MODEL, SIMULATED or REPORTED.

- Simulation mode: one laptop can demo the whole multi-device story with simulated crew, a rover and a dust storm.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It turns scattered orbital and surface datasets into one decision: go, adjust or return. It works with no Earth link, which is the real constraint on Mars. Labelling where each number comes from builds appropriate trust in the data. The same pattern could apply to lunar Artemis EVAs and to field teams on Earth in remote areas.

TOOLS

JavaScript (browser engine, Leaflet 1.9.4 offline map, Node.js hub with ws), Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio data pipeline), Capacitor 7 for the Android APK, and GitHub Actions for CI, APK builds and Pages. 138 automated tests, including a LAN end-to-end test through the real hub.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

We treated the map as a shared, living field log rather than a static viewer. We followed the communication delay, suit physiology (NASA metabolic limits), offline operation, glove-friendly mobile UI, and ISO 7010 / ANSI Z535 safety signage. We also state the honest limits: radiation values are relative, the 8,100 uGy dose was measured at Gale and not Jezero, suit parameters are nominal, and the geologic map is regional and pre-landing.
